title: Industrial Dependency Evidence Release 004: Interconnect and Data Movement
description: Research-candidate findings on how data moves in AI systems: on-package fabric, memory versus device-interconnect bandwidth, CXL host interfaces, accelerator fabrics (AMD Instinct MI300X as the primary case, NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 as a bounded contrast) and scale-out networking. Every bandwidth figure carries its unit, direction, scope and basis. Nothing in this file is a published Atlas relationship; every candidate requires named human review before it may be moved into data/dependency-atlas.json.
rights_note: Classification, unit normalisation, arithmetic and analysis are original project work by AIElectronicChips.com (Sohadot). Quoted passages are short excerpts (at most 20 words each, 40 per citation) reproduced for citation and verification; the underlying texts and specifications remain the property of their publishers. No endorsement by AMD, NVIDIA, the CXL Consortium or the Ultra Ethernet Consortium is implied. This file is a research candidate: it is visible in the public repository but is excluded from the published website.

findings.statement: AMD states that CDNA 3 uses its 4th Gen Infinity architecture fabric more extensively inside the package. It says each XCD's L2 connects to its I/O die over sixteen 64-byte channels, 1 KB per XCD at the IOD interface, and that Infinity Fabric ties the package's components together over a 4 TB/s fabric.

evidence.locator: Communication and scaling section: "fabric more prolifically inside the package"; memory section: "for a total of 1K-bytes per XCD at the IOD interface"; conclusion: "ties together all the components over a massive 4TB/s fabric"

findings.scope: On-package data movement in AMD Instinct MI300 Series, as described by AMD
limitations: The 4 TB/s figure has no stated direction, clock or measurement basis
On-package fabric bandwidth is a different domain from GPU-to-GPU link bandwidth; die-to-die integration itself is covered by the packaging reference (IDE-003)

quantities.quantity: Infinity Fabric bandwidth tying package components together

findings.statement: AMD gives MI300 Series on-package bandwidths at three tiers: up to 34.4 TB/s aggregate L2 read bandwidth, 17.2 TB/s peak from the Infinity Cache, and 5.3 TB/s peak HBM3 memory bandwidth. A figure legend in the same paper labels L2-to-XCD bandwidth 51.6 TB/s (aggregate), a scope the text does not reconcile with 34.4 TB/s.

evidence.locator: "up to 34.4 TB/s aggregate read bandwidth"; "The peak bandwidth from the Infinity Cache is an astounding 17.2 TB/s"; Figure 6 legend: "51.6 TB/s (Aggregate)"; table: "up to 5.3 TB/sec"

findings.scope: MI300 Series cache and memory bandwidth tiers as AMD states them
limitations: Read-only, aggregate and peak figures are mixed in AMD's own presentation
The 34.4 and 51.6 TB/s L2 figures are recorded as stated, not reconciled

findings.statement: AMD derives MI300X's peak memory bandwidth arithmetically: an 8,192-bit memory bus at a 5.2 Gbps data rate, divided by eight, for a total peak of 5.325 TB/s.

evidence.locator: Footnote MI300-13: "MI300X memory bus interface is 8,192"; "memory data rate is 5.2 Gbps for total peak memory bandwidth of 5.325 TB/s"

findings.scope: MI300X HBM3 peak theoretical bandwidth, AMD Performance Labs calculation as of 2023-11-07
limitations: A peak theoretical calculation, not a measured or application bandwidth

findings.statement: In one post (2026-07-21), NVIDIA states for the Rubin GPU: up to 22 TB/s of peak HBM4 bandwidth, 3,600 GB/s of NVLink 6 scale-up bandwidth to the NVLink Switch, 1,800 GB/s of NVLink-C2C bandwidth for coherent CPU-GPU communication, and up to 256 GB/s of host connectivity over x16 PCIe Gen 6.

evidence.locator: "to deliver up to 22 TB/s of peak bandwidth"; "NVIDIA NVLink 6 provides 3,600 GB/s scale-up bandwidth to the NVLink Switch"; "NVLink-C2C delivers 1,800 GB/s"; "x16 PCIe Gen 6 provides up to 256 GB/s of host connectivity"

findings.scope: Rubin GPU interface figures as stated by NVIDIA on 2026-07-21
limitations: NVIDIA's later post (2026-11-05) gives 19.2 TB/s for Rubin memory bandwidth; the HBM reference records that conflict unresolved
This post states no direction for the NVLink, NVLink-C2C or PCIe figures

quantities.quantity: NVLink 6 scale-up bandwidth to the NVLink Switch

findings.statement: NVIDIA states NVLink 6 bandwidth per Rubin GPU differently across dated posts. On 2026-01-05 it gives 3.6 TB/s of bidirectional GPU-to-GPU bandwidth per GPU. On 2026-07-21 it gives 3,600 GB/s of scale-up bandwidth. On 2026-11-05 it says each Rubin GPU brings 3.0 TB/s of NVLink 6 bandwidth.

evidence.locator: "NVIDIA NVLink 6 delivers 3.6 TB/s of bidirectional GPU-to-GPU bandwidth per GPU"
"NVIDIA NVLink 6 provides 3,600 GB/s scale-up bandwidth to the NVLink Switch"
"Each Rubin GPU brings up to 288 GB of HBM4 and 3.0 TB/s of NVLink 6 bandwidth"

findings.scope: Per-GPU NVLink 6 bandwidth as stated by NVIDIA, 2026-01-05 to 2026-11-05
limitations: The 3.0 TB/s figure has no stated direction; it was still on the live page on 2026-11-09
This release records the conflict and does not reconcile it

findings.statement: The CXL Consortium describes CXL as multiplexing three protocols: CXL.io, based on PCIe, for I/O; CXL.cache for caching; and CXL.memory for memory semantics. It says CXL maintains a unified, coherent memory space between the host CPU and memory on an attached CXL device.

evidence.locator: "I/O (CXL.io, based on PCIe), caching (CXL.cache), and memory (CXL.memory) semantics"; "CXL maintains a unified, coherent memory space between the CPU (host processor) and any memory on the attached CXL device"

findings.scope: CXL protocol layering as described in the consortium's CXL 3.0 white paper
limitations: A description of what the specification provides, not of any product's behaviour

findings.statement: The CXL 3.0 white paper says CXL 3.0, based on PCIe 6.0 technology, doubles the transfer rate to 64 GT/s, for aggregate raw bandwidth of up to 256 GB/s on an x16 link, using 256-byte flits on PAM-4 signalling.

evidence.locator: "CXL 3.0, which is based on PCIe 6.0 technology, doubles the transfer rate to 64GT/s"; "aggregate raw bandwidth of up to 256GB/s for x16 width link"; "256B flits on PAM-4 signaling"

findings.scope: CXL 3.0 physical rate and raw bandwidth as described by the consortium
limitations: 'Raw' excludes flit, FEC and protocol overhead; the white paper does not state payload bandwidth
The PCIe 6.0 basis is the consortium's statement; PCI-SIG documents could not be retrieved

quantities.quantity: aggregate raw bandwidth of an x16 link

findings.statement: The consortium distinguishes memory pooling, introduced in CXL 2.0, from memory sharing, introduced in CXL 3.0. Pooling allocates CXL-attached memory to different hosts as needed. Sharing lets a region be coherently accessed by more than one host at once using hardware coherency. It describes fabric-attached memory reachable by up to 4,095 nodes through port-based routing.

evidence.locator: "Memory pooling is the ability to treat CXL-attached memory as a fungible resource"; "Memory sharing is the ability of CXL-attached memory to be coherently shared across hosts using hardware coherency"; "accessed by multiple nodes (up to 4095)"

findings.scope: CXL 2.0 and 3.0 memory pooling and sharing as defined by the consortium
limitations: Specification capability, not evidence that any product or deployment pools or shares memory

findings.statement: The CXL Consortium announced CXL 4.0 on 2025-11-18, doubling the rate from 64 GT/s to 128 GT/s, adding bundled ports and memory RAS features, and keeping backward compatibility with earlier versions. It says members showed live demonstrations at SC25.

evidence.locator: "CXL 4.0 specification doubles bandwidth from 64GTs to 128GTs"; "Implements CXL bundled port capabilities"; "showcasing live CXL technology demonstrations at Supercomputing 2025"

findings.scope: CXL 4.0 as announced on 2025-11-18
limitations: Announcement, not the specification; the CXL 4.0 text is offered under an evaluation agreement and was not reviewed
Trade-show demonstrations are not compliance or interoperability results

findings.statement: NVIDIA lists three Vera Rubin connection types: NVLink 6 for GPU-to-GPU traffic, NVLink-C2C for coherent CPU-GPU connectivity and PCIe Gen6 for host and device integration. It states NVLink-C2C provides 1.8 TB/s of coherent bandwidth between Vera CPUs and Rubin GPUs with a unified address space, about 7x the 256 GB/s of an x16 PCIe Gen 6 link. Its CPU comparison table lists the Vera CPU with PCIe Gen6 and CXL 3.1.

evidence.locator: "PCIe Gen6 for host and device integration"; "Second-generation NVLink-C2C provides 1.8 TB/s of coherent bandwidth between Vera CPUs and Rubin GPUs"; Table 1: "Gen6/CXL 3.1"
"roughly 7x the 256 GB/s of an x16 PCIe Gen 6 link"

findings.scope: Vera Rubin host and CPU-GPU connectivity as stated by NVIDIA
limitations: CXL 3.1 is listed for the Vera CPU, not for the Rubin GPU; no CXL device behaviour or test result is described
No direction is stated for the 1.8 TB/s or 256 GB/s figures

findings.statement: AMD states that CDNA 3 communication links operate at up to 32 Gbps and that each I/O die has two 16-lane, bidirectional Infinity Fabric links to other AMD accelerators. One of those links can instead act as an x16 PCIe Gen 5 link. For MI300X, its specification table lists seven x16 Infinity Fabric links and one x16 PCIe Gen 5 link to the host CPU.

evidence.locator: "communication links have been systematically enhanced to operate at up to 32Gbps"; "Each IOD includes two 16-lane, bi-directional inter-package AMD Infinity Fabric links"; table: "7 x16 AMD Infinity Fabric™ links"

findings.scope: MI300X external links as described by AMD
limitations: AMD does not state whether 32 Gbps is a per-lane rate or what encoding the links use
Infinity Fabric is AMD's proprietary interface; no third-party interoperability is described

findings.statement: AMD states that MI300X GPUs use seven Infinity Fabric links to form a fully connected 8-GPU system, each GPU also connected to the host CPU by an x16 PCIe Gen 5 link, on the OCP Universal Base Board form factor. Its table gives a P2P ring peak aggregate I/O bandwidth of 896 GB/s, labelled '8 GPUs', and a total peak aggregate I/O bandwidth of 1024 GB/s.

evidence.locator: "uses these seven highbandwidth and low-latency AMD Infinity Fabric links to form a fully connected 8-GPU system"; "connected to the host CPU via a x16 PCIe® Gen 5 link"; table: "896 GB/s (8 GPUs)"

findings.scope: AMD Instinct MI300X 8-GPU platform as described by AMD (white paper revision 2025-04-07)
limitations: AMD does not state the direction of the 896 and 1024 GB/s figures, or whether '8 GPUs' means per GPU or per platform
No switch is shown in AMD's description; whether a deployed platform adds one is outside these sources

quantities.quantity: P2P ring peak aggregate I/O bandwidth

findings.statement: NVIDIA states that Vera Rubin NVL72 connects 72 Rubin GPUs through NVLink 6 switch trays, each with four NVLink 6 switch chips. The trays form a single all-to-all topology across the rack with in-network compute for collective operations.

evidence.locator: "Each switch tray incorporates four NVLink 6 switch chips"; "NVLink 6 switch trays form a single all-to-all topology across the rack"; "in-network SHARP compute"

findings.scope: Vera Rubin NVL72 scale-up topology as described by NVIDIA on 2026-01-05
limitations: The number of switch trays and links per GPU per switch are not stated in the reviewed post
'Consistent latency and bandwidth' is NVIDIA's characterisation; no measurement is given

findings.statement: NVIDIA states that GB200 NVL72 has 130 TB/s of aggregate NVLink bandwidth, a rack-level figure, and that NVLink 6 doubles per-GPU scale-up bandwidth over the prior generation.

evidence.locator: "On GB200 NVL72, 130 TB/s of aggregate NVLink bandwidth absorbs that traffic"
"doubling per-GPU scale-up bandwidth over the prior generation"

findings.scope: NVLink aggregate and generational figures as stated by NVIDIA
limitations: An aggregate across 72 GPUs; it is not one device's bandwidth

quantities.quantity: aggregate NVLink bandwidth of GB200 NVL72

findings.statement: The Ultra Ethernet Specification v1.1 describes three network types: a frontend network, a backend scale-out network and a local scale-up network. It names AMD's XGMI, NVIDIA's NVLINK, Intel's Xe Link, switched PCI Express and CXL systems as scale-up examples. It says scale-up domains are limited to dozens or hundreds of endpoints today, against hundreds of thousands to millions for global networks.

evidence.locator: Section 1.5.1: "1. Frontend network 2. Backend scale-out network 3. Local scale-up network"; "include AMD’s XGMI, NVIDIA’s NVLINK, Intel’s Xe Link, switched PCIExpress, and CXL systems"; "limited to dozens, maybe hundreds, of endpoints today"

findings.scope: What the UE Specification v1.1 text states in its informative introduction
limitations: Informative background, not a normative requirement
Establishes what the specification says, not how any deployment is built

findings.statement: The Ultra Ethernet Specification v1.1 states that endpoint hardware interface details are out of scope, that UE is designed to support the libibverbs and libfabric v2.0 APIs, and that it does not currently address interactions across administrative domains. Its physical-layer chapter covers PHYs for 100 Gb/s and 200 Gb/s per-lane signalling.

evidence.locator: "The details of the hardware interface at the endpoint are out of scope for the UE specifications"; "UE is designed to support libibverbs and libfabric v2.0 APIs"; "UE PHYs for 100 Gb/s per Lane Signaling"

findings.scope: Scope statements and chapter structure of the UE Specification v1.1
limitations: Only introductory sections and the table of contents were read
Per-lane signalling rates are not per-port or per-device bandwidths

findings.statement: The Ultra Ethernet Consortium's 1.0 announcement (2025-06-11) presents UEC 1.0 as an Ethernet-based stack with modern RDMA for AI and HPC. It says implementations and compliance programs are already in progress and invites members to join upcoming compliance and interoperability programs.

evidence.locator: "Modern RDMA for Ethernet and IP"; "With active implementations and compliance programs already in progress"; "participate in upcoming compliance and interoperability programs"

findings.scope: UEC 1.0 as announced on 2025-06-11
limitations: Programs in progress are not compliance or interoperability results
The announcement's descriptions of interoperability and adoption are the consortium's own

findings.statement: NVIDIA states that ConnectX-9 SuperNICs give Vera Rubin NVL72 1.6 Tb/s of scale-out connectivity per GPU. It says BlueField-4 provides up to 800 Gb/s of Ethernet or InfiniBand connectivity, Spectrum-6 Ethernet switches use co-packaged optics, and DGX SuperPOD composes eight NVL72 systems with Spectrum-X Ethernet scale-out.

evidence.locator: "ConnectX-9 SuperNICs provide high-bandwidth scale-out connectivity (1.6 Tb/s per GPU)"; "delivering up to 800 Gb/s of ultra-low-latency Ethernet or InfiniBand connectivity"; "Spectrum-6 Ethernet switches using co-packaged optics"

findings.scope: Vera Rubin scale-out networking as described by NVIDIA on 2026-01-05
limitations: 1.6 Tb/s is in bits per second and has no stated direction
DGX SuperPOD is NVIDIA's reference configuration, not evidence of how any deployment is built
No reviewed source states that Spectrum-X follows the Ultra Ethernet specification

findings.statement: Medium confidence. If AMD's 32 Gb/s is a per-lane rate, an x16 Infinity Fabric link carries 512 Gb/s, or 64 GB/s, in each direction, so 128 GB/s counting both directions. Seven links then give 896 GB/s, matching AMD's P2P figure. Adding one x16 PCIe Gen 5 link at 32 GT/s gives a further 128 GB/s and a total of 1,024 GB/s, matching AMD's total. AMD's two table figures are therefore consistent with raw, both-direction sums for one GPU, before encoding and protocol overhead, and with '8 GPUs' naming the platform rather than multiplying the figure.

evidence.locator: "operate at up to 32Gbps"; table: "896 GB/s (8 GPUs)"; "1024 GB/s"

findings.scope: Arithmetic consistency check of AMD's MI300X link figures
limitations: Consistency is not confirmation: AMD does not state per-link bandwidth or direction
Raw figures exclude encoding and protocol overhead; effective bandwidth is lower and not disclosed

quantities.quantity: x16 link raw bandwidth, both directions
seven links plus one x16 PCIe Gen 5 link, both directions

assumptions: 32 Gbps is a per-lane, per-direction raw rate
PCIe Gen 5 runs at 32 GT/s per lane

findings.statement: Medium confidence. Memory bandwidth and fabric bandwidth are different quantities, but their ratio shows how much faster a GPU reaches its own memory than its peers. For MI300X, 5.3 TB/s peak HBM3 against 896 GB/s of total fabric bandwidth is about 6x. Against the 128 GB/s of the single link joining two GPUs in AMD's mesh, it is about 41x. For Rubin, 22 TB/s, or the later 19.2 TB/s, against 3.6 TB/s of bidirectional NVLink 6 is about 5x to 6x. Through NVIDIA's switches that NVLink bandwidth can reach any peer.

evidence.locator: table: "up to 5.3 TB/sec"; "896 GB/s (8 GPUs)"
"to deliver up to 22 TB/s of peak bandwidth"
"bandwidth rose to 19.2 TB/s"
"3.6 TB/s of bidirectional GPU-to-GPU bandwidth per GPU"; "allowing any GPU to communicate with any other GPU"

findings.scope: Ratio of vendor-stated peak memory bandwidth to vendor-stated fabric bandwidth, per GPU
limitations: HBM bandwidth is a combined read/write capability, not a both-direction sum; the ratios compare different measurement domains
Peak figures only; no effective or application bandwidth was reviewed
The 128 GB/s per-pair figure depends on the assumptions in i-an-mi300x-link-arithmetic

quantities.quantity: one MI300X peer link, both directions

assumptions: AMD's 896 GB/s is a per-GPU, both-direction sum (see i-an-mi300x-link-arithmetic)
Ratios are of stated peaks and say nothing about achieved throughput

findings.statement: Medium confidence. The two documented systems reach their scale-up domains differently. In AMD's MI300X platform, each GPU dedicates one of its seven links to each of seven peers, so the domain is fixed at eight GPUs by the link count and each pair shares one link. In NVIDIA's NVL72, GPUs connect to switch trays and the trays form an all-to-all fabric of 72 GPUs, so the domain is set by switch silicon and rack design. A direct mesh avoids a switch-chip dependency but caps the domain. A switched fabric widens the domain but adds a dependency on switch chips, which in NVL72 NVIDIA also supplies. This is a structural comparison, not a performance ranking.

evidence.locator: "seven highbandwidth and low-latency AMD Infinity Fabric links to form a fully connected 8-GPU system"
"Each switch tray incorporates four NVLink 6 switch chips"; "NVLink 6 switch trays form a single all-to-all topology across the rack"

findings.scope: Topology comparison of two vendor-documented scale-up designs
limitations: No measured collective or all-to-all throughput was reviewed for either system
Different generations and dates: MI300X (2023) and Vera Rubin NVL72 (2026)
assumptions: The vendor descriptions are complete for the scale-up domain they describe

findings.statement: Medium confidence. Several stated figures cannot be compared until units and directions are aligned. NVIDIA's 3.6 TB/s NVLink 6 figure is in bytes and bidirectional, equal to 28.8 Tb/s. Its 1.6 Tb/s ConnectX-9 figure is in bits with no direction, equal to 200 GB/s. Per GPU, scale-up therefore exceeds scale-out about 9x if 1.6 Tb/s is per direction, or 18x if it counts both directions. For CXL 3.0, 64 GT/s across 16 lanes is 1,024 Gb/s, or 128 GB/s per direction before overhead. The consortium's 256 GB/s 'aggregate raw' figure therefore counts both directions, as does NVIDIA's 256 GB/s for x16 PCIe Gen 6 if it uses the same basis.

evidence.locator: "3.6 TB/s of bidirectional GPU-to-GPU bandwidth per GPU"; "(1.6 Tb/s per GPU)"
"doubles the transfer rate to 64GT/s"; "aggregate raw bandwidth of up to 256GB/s for x16 width link"
"the 256 GB/s of an x16 PCIe Gen 6 link"

findings.scope: Unit and direction normalisation of vendor and consortium figures
limitations: Arithmetic conversion only; real payload throughput after flit, FEC and protocol overhead is lower and not disclosed
NVIDIA does not state the basis of its 256 GB/s PCIe figure
assumptions: One transfer carries one bit per lane before encoding
8 bits per byte; no overhead subtracted

findings.statement: Medium confidence. Leaving the scale-up domain changes the dependency model, not only the bandwidth. Inside NVL72, GPU-to-GPU traffic runs over NVIDIA's NVLink switches. Beyond the rack it runs over NICs, Ethernet switches and optics. NVIDIA's own reference design uses ConnectX-9, Spectrum-X and Spectrum-6 with co-packaged optics, and the UE specification describes the backend scale-out network as a separate network with its own transport. The scale-out tier therefore adds NIC, switch, optics and network-software dependencies that the scale-up fabric does not have. The reviewed sources do not show which of those components are interchangeable in practice.

evidence.locator: "Spectrum-X Ethernet extends that capability beyond the rack"; "Spectrum-6 Ethernet switches using co-packaged optics"
"The backend network is usually a specialized high-performance network of limited scope relative to the frontend network"

findings.scope: Structural change in dependencies between scale-up and scale-out tiers
limitations: No deployment, supplier-availability or performance inference is made
UEC membership or specification release does not establish that any named product follows the specification
assumptions: The documented NVIDIA reference design is representative of how a scale-out tier is added

unresolved.question: Is Rubin's per-GPU NVLink 6 bandwidth 3.6 TB/s bidirectional or 3.0 TB/s, and what does the 3.0 TB/s figure measure?
unresolved.why_unresolved: NVIDIA states 3.6 TB/s bidirectional (2026-01-05) and 3,600 GB/s (2026-07-21), then 3.0 TB/s with no direction (2026-11-05). None of the posts labels either figure preliminary.
unresolved.next_evidence_needed: An NVIDIA datasheet or specification stating the per-GPU NVLink 6 figure, its direction and any configuration dependence.

unresolved.question: What are the per-link bandwidth, direction and encoding of MI300X's Infinity Fabric links, and is the 896 GB/s figure per GPU?
unresolved.why_unresolved: AMD gives 32 Gbps links, seven x16 links and an 896 GB/s 'P2P ring peak aggregate' labelled '8 GPUs', but states no per-link figure or direction. The arithmetic is consistent with a per-GPU, both-direction sum, but it is not confirmed.
unresolved.next_evidence_needed: AMD documentation stating Infinity Fabric per-link bandwidth, direction and encoding for MI300X.

unresolved.question: How do AMD's 34.4 TB/s aggregate L2 read bandwidth and the 51.6 TB/s L2-to-XCD figure in its legend relate?
unresolved.why_unresolved: Both appear in the same white paper with different labels, and the text does not reconcile them.
unresolved.next_evidence_needed: AMD clarification of each figure's scope, for example read-only versus read plus write.

unresolved.question: What collective or application bandwidth do the MI300X 8-GPU platform and Vera Rubin NVL72 achieve in practice?
unresolved.why_unresolved: All reviewed figures are vendor-stated peaks. No measured all-reduce, all-to-all or application bandwidth with a stated method was reviewed.
unresolved.next_evidence_needed: Measured results with disclosed workload, message sizes and method, from a vendor technical paper or independent study.

unresolved.question: What latencies do these fabrics achieve, under what workloads and measurement methods?
unresolved.why_unresolved: NVIDIA describes 'consistent latency' and the UE specification describes sub-microsecond targets for scale-up networks, but no reviewed source gives a measured latency with method.

unresolved.question: What do the PCI-SIG PCIe 6.0 and 7.0 specifications and announcements state about rates, encoding and payload efficiency?
unresolved.why_unresolved: pcisig.com refused automated access (HTTP 403). PCIe figures here come only from the CXL Consortium and GPU vendors.
unresolved.next_evidence_needed: PCI-SIG announcements or specification summaries read directly.

unresolved.question: Do MI300X or Rubin GPUs implement CXL, and which device type and coherency behaviour would apply?
unresolved.why_unresolved: The reviewed AMD sources do not mention CXL for MI300X. NVIDIA lists CXL 3.1 for the Vera CPU, not the Rubin GPU, and describes no CXL device behaviour.
unresolved.next_evidence_needed: Product documentation naming CXL support and device type, and compliance or interoperability results.

unresolved.question: What do the normative CXL 3.x and 4.0 specifications require for coherency, sharing and the 128 GT/s physical layer?
unresolved.why_unresolved: The CXL 4.0 text is offered under an evaluation agreement, which was not accepted. Only the CXL 3.0 cover page was opened; announcements and a white paper were read.
unresolved.next_evidence_needed: A reviewer reads the relevant CXL specification sections.

unresolved.question: Which products comply with the Ultra Ethernet specification, and have multi-vendor interoperability results been published?
unresolved.why_unresolved: UEC describes compliance programs as in progress or upcoming. No reviewed source names a compliant product or a test result, and NVIDIA does not state that Spectrum-X follows the specification.
unresolved.next_evidence_needed: Published UEC compliance or interoperability results naming products.

unresolved.question: What optical link counts, reach and reliability apply to co-packaged-optics switches in deployed AI clusters?
unresolved.why_unresolved: NVIDIA states that Spectrum-6 uses co-packaged optics but gives no link counts, reach or field data in the reviewed post.
unresolved.next_evidence_needed: Switch datasheets and published field-reliability data.
